text:
Thoughts
expand_more
Based on William Sanday and Arthur C. Headlam's A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans (1895), the seven Romans passages among the B001 targets are directly addressed in the commentary, whereas the five non-Romans passages (from 1 Corinthians and Galatians) are NOT DISCUSSED in this commentary.
B001 Discussion Analysis Table
B001 ID
	
Discussed
	
Page / Locator
	
Depth
	
Description of Author's Discussion


1. Romans 4:3 / Genesis 15:6
	
YES
	
Pages 100–102
1
2
	
Extended
	
Sanday and Headlam analyze Paul's quotation of Genesis 15:6 (ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην), explaining the accounting metaphor of reckoning faith as righteousness and contrasting Paul's exegesis with James's reliance on Genesis 22 and rabbinic traditions of Abrahamic merit
1
2
.


2. Romans 9:25 / Hosea 2:23
	
YES
	
Page 264
3
	
Substantive
	
The authors examine Paul's textual modifications in Hosea 2:23—inverting the clauses, following Codex Vaticanus (ἀγαπήσω), and substituting καλέσω from the preceding verse—to demonstrate God's calling of the Gentiles into covenant relationship
3
.


3. Romans 9:26 / Hosea 1:10
	
YES
	
Page 264
3
	
Substantive
	
Sanday and Headlam discuss Paul's quotation of Hosea 1:10, highlighting his insertion of ἐκεῖ to emphasize the location where former outcasts are proclaimed children of God, evaluating both Palestinian and universal geographical interpretations
3
.


4. Romans 10:11 / Isaiah 28:16
	
YES
	
Page 290
4
	
Substantive
	
The authors explain that Paul re-quotes Isaiah 28:16 with the explicit addition of πᾶς ("everyone") to establish that faith in Christ is the universal condition of salvation for both Jew and Gentile
4
.


5. Romans 10:13 / Joel 2:32
	
YES
	
Page 291
5
	
Substantive
	
Sanday and Headlam detail how Paul quotes Joel 2:32 verbatim to clench his argument that salvation is universally guaranteed to anyone who calls upon the name of the Lord (applied christologically to Jesus)
5
.


6. Romans 11:34 / Isaiah 40:13
	
YES
	
Page 340
6
	
Substantive
	
The authors note that Paul's doxological question is cited directly from Isaiah 40:13 with minimal variation from the LXX (comparing 1 Cor 2:16) to affirm the unsearchable depth of God's wisdom and counsel
6
.


7. Romans 15:12 / Isaiah 11:10
	
YES
	
Page 399
7
	
Substantive
	
Sanday and Headlam analyze Paul's citation of Isaiah 11:10 following the LXX paraphrase to describe the reign of the "root of Jesse" over the Gentiles in the Messianic kingdom
7
.


8. 1 Corinthians 1:19 / Isaiah 29:14
	
NO

N/A
	
NOT DISCUSSED

citations.snippet: 100 EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS [IV. 2, 3.  paraphrase. There should be a colon after xavynpa. St. Paul does not question the supposed claim that Abraham has a καύχημα absolutely—before man he might have it and the Jews were not wrong in the veneration with which they regarded his memory,— but it was another thing to have a καύχημα before God. There is a stress upon τὸν Θεόν which is taken up by τῷ Θεῷ in the quota- tion. ‘A. could not boast before God. He might have done so if he could aave taken his stand on works; but works did not enter into the question at all. In God he put faith’ On the history and application of the text Gen. xv. 6, see below.  8. ἐλογίσθη : metaphor from accounts, ‘ was set down,’ here ‘on the credit side.’ Frequently in LXX with legal sense of imputation or non-imputation of guilt, e.g. Lev. vii. 8 ἐὰν δὲ φαγὼν φάγῃ . .. οὐ λογισθήσεται αὐτῷ, XVil. 4 λογισθήσεται τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκείνῳ αἷμα, &C. The notion arises from that of the ‘ book of remembrance’ (Mal. iii. 16) in which men’s good or evil deeds, the wrongs, and sufferings of the saints, are entered (Ps. lvi. 8; Is. Ixv. 6). Oriental monarchs had such a record by which they were reminded of the merit or demerit of their subjects (Esth. vi. 1 ff.), and in like manner on the judgement day Jehovah would have the ‘books’ brought out before Him (Dan. vii. 10; Rev. xx. 12; comp. also ‘the books of the living,’ ‘ the heavenly tablets,’ a common expres- sion in the Books of Enoch, Jubilees, and Test. XII Pair., on which see Charles on Loch xlvii. 3; and in more modern times, Cowper’s sonnet ‘ There is a book . . . wherein the eyes of God not rarely look’).  The idea of imputation in this sense was familiar to the Jews (Weber, Al/syn. Theol. p. 233). They had also the idea of the transference of merit and demerit from one person to another (δια. p. 280 ff.; Ezek. xviii. 2; John ix. 2). That however is not in question here; the point is that one quality faith is set down, or credited, to the individual (here to Abraham) in place of another quality—righteousness.  ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην : was reckoned as equivalent to, as standing in the place of, ‘righteousness. The construction is common in LXX: cf. 1 Reg. (Sam.) i. 13; Job xli. 23 (24); Is. xxix. 17 (= xxxii. 15; Lam. iv. 2; Hos. viii. 12. The exact phrase ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσ. recurs in Ps. cv [cvi]. 31 of the zeal of Phinehas. On the grammar cf. Win. ὃ xxix. 3 a. (p. 229,  ed. Moulton). On the righteousness of Abraham see esp. Weber, A/ésyn. Palast.  Theologie, p. 255 ff. Abraham was the only righteous man of his generation; therefore he was chosen to be ancestor of the holy People. He kept all the precepts of the Law which he knew beforehand by a kind of intuition. He was the first of seven righteous men whose merit brought back the Shekinah which had

It is at first sight a remarkable thing that two New Testament writers should use the same leading example and should quote the same leading text as it would seem to directly opposite effect. We notice at once that St. Paul keeps more strictly to his text. Gen. xv. 6 speaks only of faith. St. James supports his contention of the necessity of works by appeal to a later incident in Abraham’s life, the offering of Isaac (Jas. ii. 21). St. Paul also appeals to particular incidents, Abraham’s belief in the promise that he should have a numerous progeny (Rom. iv. 18), and in the more express prediction of the birth of Isaac (Rom. iv. I9-21). The difference  is that St. Paul makes use of a more searching exegesis. His own spiritual experience confirms the unqualified affirmation of the Book of Genesis; and he is therefore able to take it as one of the foundations of his system, St. James, occupying a less exceptional

The LXX reads ἐλεήσω τὴν οὐκ ἠλεημένην, καὶ ἐρῶ τῷ οὐ λαῷ μου Λαός μου  εἶ σύ, but for the first clause which agrees with the Hebrew the Vatican  substitutes ὠγαπήσω τὴν οὐκ ἠγαπημένην. St. Paul inverts the order of the  clauses, so that the reference to τὸν οὐ λαόν pov, which seems particularly to  suit the Gentiles, comes first, and for ἐρῶ substitutes καλέσω which naturally  crept in from the ἐκάλεσεν of the previous verse, and changes the construc-  tion of the clause to suit the new word. Rom. iii. το.
